flags.text: Check: The CTA uses the word 'free' but never states the 14-day trial length as required.
Check: Claiming the product reads a user's inbox, texts and calendar is a sensitive data-access claim that may need privacy/compliance qualification before it's inherited by all markets.
Check: 'Kin reads your inbox and your calendar' is a data access claim; UK audiences are alert to data rights and may push back unless purpose and control are made clear.
Check: The free trial claim doesn't address what happens when the 14 days end, which may run into incoming DMCC subscription-contract rules that aren't confirmed here.

Check: 'Kin keeps track of your inbox and calendar' is a data-access claim. Given NG-S3's note that online fraud is a live concern, this needs clear purpose and control framing so it doesn't read as intrusive access to messages.
Check: The same inbox/calendar access claim should be checked against NDPA requirements that ads not overstate or obscure what data the product actually accesses and on what lawful basis.

Check: The variant drops 'your inbox, your texts' from the data-access line, keeping only 'reads your calendar.' If Kin still processes messages, omitting this could read as understating what the product accesses.
Check: There's no ZA-specific guidance on how an AI assistant reading personal data is perceived locally, so the calendar-only claim may still need extra reassurance on scope and control.
